title: Reentrancy Attack: 1 Withdraw → 10 Withdrawals 🐍
ig_caption:
Stop scrolling: one bug can drain a vault by calling withdraw again.
Reentrancy turns “send ETH” into an infinite loophole.

• Vault.sol is VULNERABLE
• withdraw() reads your balance: uint amt = balances[msg.sender]
• ① It sends ETH out first: msg.sender.call{value: amt}("")
• ② Only after sending, it updates the ledger: balances[msg.sender] = 0
• DEPTH 0 → the attacker’s fallback executes during the ETH transfer
• Reentrancy: the attacker calls withdraw() again before balances are set to 0
• Result: “One withdraw” becomes “Ten withdrawals” (iterative drains)

Practical Takeaway: In DeFi, always update internal state (effects) before external calls (interactions). Prefer checks-effects-interactions and use reentrancy guards.

What’s riskier to your funds: sending ETH before zeroing balances, or trusting external contracts? 👇

fb_caption:
Reentrancy isn’t just a classic Solidity mistake—it’s a systemic security failure pattern that shows up whenever a contract:
1) makes an external call, and
2) still relies on its internal accounting not being changed yet.

In the animation (Vault.sol · VULNERABLE):
- withdraw() starts by loading balances[msg.sender] into amt.
- It performs an external interaction first: msg.sender.call{value: amt}("").
- Only after the call returns does it update the ledger: balances[msg.sender] = 0.

Why this is catastrophic:
- call{value: amt} hands control to msg.sender.
- If msg.sender is an attacker contract, its fallback/receive function can immediately call withdraw() again.
- Because balances[msg.sender] hasn’t been zeroed yet, the second (and third… and tenth) withdrawal still passes the same balance checks.
- The “DEPTH 0 → depth N” effect is the attacker repeatedly re-entering before state changes finalize.

Protocol/security implications (trade-offs):
- Checks-Effects-Interactions: Move balance updates before external calls. This removes the “stale state” window.
- ReentrancyGuard: Adds a cheap mutex to block nested withdraw calls.
- Pull over push payments: Designing withdrawals as user-initiated pulls (with safe accounting) reduces reliance on fragile transfer flows.
- Tokenomics impact: While reentrancy doesn’t mint tokens by itself, it can drain reserves/ETH backing, causing insolvency-like outcomes. That translates to price impact, forced deleveraging, and downstream liquidity shocks.

Alpha takeaway: Audit reentrancy paths by scanning for any external call (call/transfer/delegatecall) that happens before critical state updates. If you see “send first, zero later,” treat it as a red-flag until proven otherwise.

What do you think should be the default in production DeFi: reentrancy guards everywhere, or rely purely on CEI ordering? Drop your take—let’s debate.
